blocks.text: **Clock problems** deal with the **angle between the hour and minute hands** and the **times they coincide, are opposite, or at right angles**. The minute hand moves 360° per hour; the hour hand 30° per hour — a relative speed of **5.5° per minute**.

items: **Angle = |30H − 5.5M|**; if >180°, subtract from 360°.
Hands **coincide (0°)**: 11 times/12 hrs; **opposite (180°)**: 11 times/12 hrs.
Hands are at **right angles (90°)**: 22 times/12 hrs.
A clock gaining/losing time: track **error per 12/24 hrs**.
Clock = 360°; **minute hand 6°/min**, **hour hand 0.5°/min**; minute hand gains **5.5°/min** over hour hand.
**Angle between hands** = |30·H − 5.5·M|° (H=hour, M=minutes).
Hands **coincide** every **65 5/11 min** (~22 times/day); at **right angles/straight line** twice per hour except overlaps.
A clock **too fast/slow** — compute gain/loss over 24 h.

prelimsPointers: Angle between hands = **|30H − 5.5M|** degrees.
Minute hand = **6°/min**, hour hand = **0.5°/min**, relative = **5.5°/min**.
Hands **coincide 11 times / 12 hours** (22 times a day).
Hands at **90° → 22 times / 12 hours**; opposite (180°) → 11 times.
In **65 5⁄11 minutes** the hands coincide once.
A 'faulty' clock problem = compare gained/lost minutes over a period.
**Angle = |30H − 5.5M|°**; minute hand gains **5.5°/min**.
Hands coincide every **65 5/11 min** → **11 times / 12 hours** (22/day).
Minute hand **6°/min**, hour hand **0.5°/min**.
Right angle 2×/hour (except near overlaps).

glossary.definition: The minute hand gains 5.5° per minute over the hour hand.
When both hands overlap (0° apart) — 11 times every 12 hours.

blocks.text: **Calendar problems** find the **day of the week** for a given date using **odd days** — the remainder days over complete weeks. Leap-year rules and month codes are the key tools.

items: A **leap year** is divisible by 4; centuries must be divisible by **400** (2000 is leap, 1900 is not).
Count total **odd days** up to the date, then map to a weekday.
**Same calendar** repeats after a cycle (e.g. usually 28, 6, 11 or 5 years apart).
A leap year adds **2 odd days**, an ordinary year **1**.
**Odd days**: remainder when days ÷ 7; ordinary year = **1 odd day**, leap year = **2**; **century** — 100 yrs=5, 200=3, 300=1, 400=0 odd days.
**Leap year**: divisible by 4 (century must be ÷400: 2000 leap, 1900 not).
**Day of week**: count odd days from a known reference; 0=Sunday,1=Mon…6=Sat.
**Same calendar repeats**: after 6/11/28 years depending on leap position.
**Doomsday/reference**: 1 Jan 1 AD basis — total odd days give the day.

blocks.text: Solved: 1900 is **not** a leap year (century not ÷400). || A year has 365 days = 52 weeks + **1 odd day** → next year same date shifts one weekday (two after a leap year).

prelimsPointers: **Ordinary year = 1 odd day; leap year = 2 odd days**.
**Leap year** = divisible by 4; a **century** must be divisible by **400** (2000 leap; 1900 not).
Map odd days: **0=Sunday, 1=Monday … 6=Saturday**.
**Doomsday/reference-day** methods speed up day-finding.
A given calendar repeats after a fixed cycle of years.
**Odd days**: ordinary yr=1, leap=2; **100 yrs=5, 400 yrs=0** odd days.
**Leap**: ÷4 (century needs ÷400 — 2000 leap, 1900 not).
Day count: **0=Sun … 6=Sat**.
Date shifts **1 weekday** each ordinary year (2 across a leap year).

glossary.definition: The days left over beyond complete weeks, used to find the weekday of a date.
A 366-day year (divisible by 4, centuries by 400) adding 2 odd days.

blocks.text: **Age problems** translate verbal statements about people's ages into **linear equations**. The key is defining a variable for the present age and expressing past/future ages by adding or subtracting years.

rows: Age difference stays constant over time.

items: Let the **present age = x** (or use ratio multiples).
Write **past = x − t** and **future = x + t**.
Form and solve the **linear equation(s)**.
Remember: the **difference between two ages never changes**.

sections.heading: 🕐 Formulae & solved examples: problems on ages

items: Represent ages with a variable; **'x years ago'** subtract x from each, **'x years hence'** add.
Ratio of ages changes over time — set up equations from two time-points.
**Sum/difference stays**: age difference between two people is **constant** over time.
Average-age problems: total age = average × number of persons.

blocks.text: Solved: Father is 3× son now; in 12 yrs he'll be 2× → 3x+12 = 2(x+12) → x = 12, father = **36**. || The difference in ages never changes: if A−B = 8 now, it's 8 forever.

prelimsPointers: '**years ago**' → subtract; '**years hence**' → add.
The **difference between two people's ages is constant** over time.
For **ratio** ages, use a common multiplier (3k, 5k) and solve.
Translate each clause into an **equation**, then solve simultaneously.
Check the answer against **all** conditions in the problem.
**Age difference between two people is constant** across time.
'x years ago' → subtract x; 'x years hence' → add x, then form equations.
Ratio problems: use **two time-points** to solve.
Total age = **average × number of persons**.

glossary.definition: An equation of the first degree used to model age relationships.
The fact that the gap between two ages remains the same at all times.
